title: Plugin lifecycle hooks fire only once: signal listener deletes the whole hook array
summary: After a lifecycle signal is delivered, the listener deletes `sdk.__hooks[type]`, destroying every registered hook for that lifecycle type. All subsequent signals of the same type find no hooks and silently do nothing.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `onPluginActive(() => refreshData())`. The first time CoreBox activates the plugin the callback runs and `__hooks['ac']` is deleted. On every later activation the transport listener still fires but `hooksMap['ac']` is undefined, so `refreshData()` is never called again -> the plugin shows stale data for the rest of the session with no error.
recommendation: Do not delete the hook array after dispatch; keep hooks registered for the lifetime of the plugin and only remove them on explicit unsubscribe.

title: onPluginActive/onPluginInactive documented boolean veto is never honoured
summary: JSDoc for `onPluginActive`/`onPluginInactive` promises `If return false, the plugin will not be activated`, but the hook's return value is discarded by `wrappedHook` and the default processor always calls `reply(true)`.
failure_scenario: A plugin implements `onPluginActive(() => { if (!licenseValid) return false })` to block activation while unlicensed. `hook(data)` result is thrown away and `processFunc` replies `true` unconditionally, so the plugin activates anyway - the documented gate silently does nothing.
recommendation: Collect hook return values in `wrappedHook` and pass `hooks.every(h => h(data) !== false)` into `reply`, or remove the veto claim from the JSDoc.

title: Lifecycle signal transport listener is never unsubscribed and re-registers per hook cycle
summary: `transport.on()` returns an unsubscribe function that is discarded. Combined with the `delete sdk.__hooks[type]` above, every re-registration after a delivered signal sees `hooks.length === 0` and attaches an additional listener for the same event.
failure_scenario: A plugin re-registers `onPluginActive` on each of its own view mounts. After the first activate signal the hook array is deleted, so the next `injectHook` sees length 0 and adds a second transport listener while the first stays attached. After N mount cycles, N listeners fire per signal and none can ever be removed.
recommendation: Store and invoke the unsubscribe function, and guard registration with a per-type `registered` flag rather than `hooks.length === 0`.

title: Plugin channel replies serialize the raw IpcRendererEvent, which is not structured-cloneable
summary: `__parse_raw_data` stores the live `IpcRendererEvent` on `header.event`, and `__parse_sender` copies it straight into the reply object handed to `ipcRenderer.send`. `IpcRendererEvent` carries `sender`/`ports` and cannot survive structured clone.
failure_scenario: A plugin registers any synchronous channel handler. When the main process sends a request, `handInData.reply(DataCode.SUCCESS, res)` calls `ipcRenderer.send` with an object graph containing the original `IpcRendererEvent` -> Electron throws `An object could not be cloned`, the reply is never delivered, and the main-process caller hangs until its timeout.
recommendation: Strip `header.event` (and `_originData`) before constructing the reply payload; keep the event only in local scope.

title: Async plugin channel handlers never send a reply, hanging the main-process caller
summary: When a registered handler returns a Promise, `__handle_main` returns early and never awaits it, so `reply()` is never invoked for asynchronous handlers.
failure_scenario: A plugin registers `channel.regChannel('do-work', async (d) => await compute(d))`. The handler resolves normally but no reply is ever sent, so the main process's pending sync request for `do-work` sits in `pendingMap` until the 60s `CHANNEL_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` fires and rejects.
recommendation: Await the promise and reply with its resolved value, replying with an error code when it rejects.

title: Unguarded JSON.parse in the plugin IPC listener throws on non-string payloads
summary: `__handle_main` assumes the IPC argument is always a JSON string, but `send()` in the same class posts a plain object on the same `@plugin-process-message` channel. Any non-string or malformed payload throws out of the IPC listener.
evidence:
__handle_main(e: IpcRendererEvent, _arg: any): any {
    const arg = JSON.parse(_arg);
failure_scenario: The main process (or a loopback of this class's own `send`, which posts an object at line 300) delivers an object rather than a JSON string. `JSON.parse` coerces it to `"[object Object]"` and throws `SyntaxError`, which escapes the ipcRenderer listener as an uncaught exception in the plugin renderer and drops every message on that channel.
recommendation: Wrap the parse in try/catch and accept objects directly: `const arg = typeof _arg === 'string' ? safeParse(_arg) : _arg`.

title: TuffRendererTransport.destroy() leaves every on() channel listener registered
summary: `on()` registers a listener with the underlying channel and returns its cleanup to the caller without storing it. `destroy()` only clears the `handlers` map, so all channel-level registrations survive and keep invoking handlers after the transport is destroyed.
failure_scenario: A renderer view creates a transport, calls `transport.on(AppEvents.x, handler)`, then calls `transport.destroy()` on unmount without holding the per-handler cleanup. The channel registration remains, so `handler` keeps firing on every subsequent main-process broadcast, touching torn-down component state and leaking the closure for the lifetime of the window.
recommendation: Collect the `cleanup` returned by `this.channel.regChannel` per handler and invoke all of them in `destroy()`.

title: Response cache and batch dedupe collide on non-serializable payloads, returning another call's result
summary: `buildCacheKey` and `buildBatchKey` fall back to `Object.prototype.toString.call(payload)` when `JSON.stringify` throws. Every circular or non-serializable object collapses to the same key, so distinct requests share one cache entry / dedupe bucket.
failure_scenario: A consumer calls `transport.send(ev, payloadA, { cache: true })` and then `transport.send(ev, payloadB, { cache: true })` where both payloads contain a circular reference. Both build the key `"<event>:[object Object]"`, so the second call silently returns payloadA's response instead of issuing a request - wrong data with no error. The same collision merges unrelated requests under `mergeStrategy: 'dedupe'`.
recommendation: Throw or bypass caching/dedupe when the payload cannot be serialized, instead of falling back to a type-only key.

title: Batching sends requests strictly sequentially, making batch-enabled events slower than unbatched
summary: Despite the `BatchPayload`/`BatchResponse` protocol types, `flushEvent` never combines requests. For the default `queue` strategy it chains each entry through `reduce(...).then(...)`, serializing what would otherwise be concurrent IPC calls.
evidence:
await queue.queue.reduce<Promise<void>>(
      (promise, entry) => promise.then(() => this.flushEntry(eventName, entry)),
      Promise.resolve(),
    )
failure_scenario: An event declared with `batch: { enabled: true, windowMs: 50, maxSize: 50 }` receives 50 concurrent `send()` calls. Instead of one batched round-trip they are queued for 50ms and then issued one-at-a-time, so total latency becomes 50ms + 50x the per-request round-trip - strictly worse than not enabling batching.
recommendation: Either issue the queued entries with `Promise.all`, or implement the declared batch envelope so the queue becomes a single request.

title: Exported BatchPayload/BatchResponse/BatchResult types describe a protocol that is never implemented
summary: `BatchPayload`, `BatchResult` and `BatchResponse` are exported from the package's public transport surface, but a repo-wide search finds no producer or consumer - no code ever builds or parses the `{ event, requests: [{id, payload}] }` envelope.
failure_scenario: An external plugin developer writes a main-process handler typed against `BatchPayload` to receive batched storage reads. At runtime the renderer sends the bare per-request payload (see `flushEntry`), so `payload.requests` is undefined and the handler throws on every batch-enabled event.
recommendation: Either implement the batch envelope end-to-end or remove these types from the public export surface.

title: usePluginStorage().onDidChange passes the event envelope instead of the new file content
summary: The callback is typed and documented as `(newConfig: any) => void`, but the listener forwards the raw update payload `{ name, fileName }` (`PluginStorageUpdatePayload`), which carries no content at all.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `storage.onDidChange('settings.json', cfg => applyTheme(cfg.theme))`. On every write it receives `{ name: 'my-plugin', fileName: 'settings.json' }`, so `cfg.theme` is `undefined` and the theme silently resets - the developer has no way to obtain the new value from the callback.
recommendation: Re-fetch via `getFile(fileName)` inside the listener before invoking the callback, or extend `PluginStorageUpdatePayload` to carry the content.

title: usePluginStorage().onDidChange fires for unrelated files when fileName is absent
summary: The subscription filter treats a missing `fileName` on the broadcast as a match for every subscribed file, so a whole-plugin storage event notifies all per-file subscribers.
failure_scenario: A plugin subscribes separately to `settings.json` and `cache.json`, then calls `clearAll()`, which broadcasts an update without `fileName`. Both subscribers fire as though their specific file changed, so each reloads and rewrites state that was just cleared.
recommendation: Treat a missing `fileName` as a distinct 'all files' signal the caller opts into, rather than matching every specific subscription.

title: setFile throws an opaque SyntaxError for undefined content
summary: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(content))` is used to strip non-cloneables, but `JSON.stringify(undefined)` returns `undefined`, and `JSON.parse(undefined)` coerces to the string `"undefined"` and throws. Circular content throws a TypeError from the same expression.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `storage.setFile('state.json', undefined)` to clear a value. Rather than the documented `{ success: false, error }` result it gets an unhandled `SyntaxError: "undefined" is not valid JSON` thrown synchronously from the SDK, which does not match the declared `Promise<{ success, error? }>` return contract.
recommendation: Guard the serialization and surface `{ success: false, error }` for non-serializable content instead of letting JSON throw.

title: @talex-touch/utils publishes raw TypeScript with no types field, exports map, or build step
summary: `main`/`module` both point at `index.ts` and there is no `types`, no `exports` map, and no build script. The published tarball in-tree contains 295 `.ts` files and 2 `.js` files, so Node cannot load the package at all.
failure_scenario: An external plugin developer runs `npm i @talex-touch/utils` and writes `require('@talex-touch/utils')` in a plain Node prelude, or `import { TuffInputType } from '@talex-touch/utils/transport'` in a bundler that does not transpile `node_modules`. Node resolves `index.ts` and fails with `SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'`; the subpath has no `index.js` to resolve at all.
recommendation: Add a build (tsup/tsc) emitting `dist/*.js` + `.d.ts`, and declare `types`, `exports` subpaths, and a `prepublishOnly` script.

title: PermissionIds constant omits the localization permissions, so PermissionId type cannot express them
summary: `PERMISSIONS` registers `i18n.read`, `lexicon.read` and `lexicon.register`, but the `PermissionIds` map - and therefore the exported `PermissionId` union used for type safety - has no entries for them.
failure_scenario: A plugin developer writes `const p: PermissionId = 'lexicon.register'` to declare a manifest permission. TypeScript rejects it as not assignable to the union even though `permissionRegistry.has('lexicon.register')` returns true at runtime, forcing a cast that defeats the constant's stated purpose ('Permission ID constants for type safety').
recommendation: Add `I18N_READ`, `LEXICON_READ`, `LEXICON_REGISTER` to `PermissionIds`, or derive the union from `PERMISSIONS` so the two cannot drift.

title: SupportOS.WATCHOS_9 and WATCHOS_10 have their values swapped
summary: The `WATCHOS_9` member is assigned the string `'watchOS 10'` and `WATCHOS_10` is assigned `'watchOS 9'`. `WINDOWS_11` is likewise assigned `'Windows 10 Pro'`.
failure_scenario: Any consumer that compares a detected OS string against `SupportOS.WATCHOS_10` matches devices running watchOS 9 and misses watchOS 10, inverting platform gating. `SupportOS.WINDOWS_11 === 'Windows 10 Pro'` similarly never matches a Windows 11 string.
recommendation: Swap the two watchOS values and correct `WINDOWS_11` to `'Windows 11'`.

title: TuffTransportError.fromJSON drops the original timestamp
summary: `toJSON` serializes `timestamp`, but `fromJSON` never restores it - the constructor unconditionally overwrites `this.timestamp` with `Date.now()` at reconstruction time.
failure_scenario: A renderer rehydrates an IPC-transported error to correlate it with a main-process log line. `err.timestamp` reads as the deserialization time rather than the moment the failure occurred, so the timestamps never line up and the round-trip is not lossless as `toJSON`/`fromJSON` imply.
recommendation: Assign `error.timestamp` from `obj.timestamp` when it is a finite number.

title: Plugin prelude channel always replies undefined, discarding every handler return value
summary: The injected prelude's `__dispatch` calls the listener and then unconditionally replies `undefined`, unlike the sibling `plugin/channel.ts` implementation which replies with the handler's result.
failure_scenario: A Prelude script registers `$channel.regChannel('get-config', () => ({ theme: 'dark' }))`. The main process awaits the reply and receives `undefined` instead of the config object, so any main-side feature that round-trips a value through a prelude handler silently reads undefined.
recommendation: Capture `const res = func(handInData)` and reply with it (awaiting when it is a promise), matching `plugin/channel.ts`.

title: Plugin prelude accepts channel messages whose header has no uniqueKey
summary: The prelude validates `header.uniqueKey` against the injected key, but a message with no `uniqueKey` at all only logs a warning and is then processed normally. Only a mismatched key is rejected.
failure_scenario: Any code able to emit on the shared `@plugin-process-message` IPC channel omits `header.uniqueKey` and its payload is dispatched to this plugin's registered handlers. The key check that is the plugin channel's isolation boundary is bypassed by simply not supplying a key.
recommendation: Treat a missing `uniqueKey` the same as a mismatch: log and `return null`.

title: Plugin prelude earlyMessageQueue grows without bound when no listener registers
summary: Messages arriving for an event with no registered listener are pushed into `earlyMessageQueue` indefinitely. The queue is only drained by a matching `regChannel` call and has no size or age cap.
failure_scenario: A plugin never registers a handler for a broadcast event the main process emits on every search keystroke. Each keystroke appends an entry (holding the full `rawData` plus the IpcRendererEvent) to the queue, so a long session grows the plugin renderer's heap without limit and never releases it.
recommendation: Cap the queue per event name and drop the oldest entries, or expire queued messages after a short window.

title: TuffPluginTransport queues unclaimed port confirms forever, pinning live MessagePorts
summary: When a confirm arrives before its `openPort` waiter, the record is stored with no expiry. The sibling renderer transport attaches a `PORT_CONFIRM_TIMEOUT_MS` timer for exactly this case and documents that omitting it pins the port for the transport's lifetime.
failure_scenario: A plugin calls `openPort` and the upgrade round-trip rejects after the main process already transferred the port. The confirm lands with no pending waiter, so the live MessagePort sits in `queuedPortConfirms` until `destroy()` - each failed open permanently leaks one native MessagePort plus its entangled main-side channel.
recommendation: Mirror the renderer transport: attach a timeout that closes the port and sends `port.close` with reason `confirm_unclaimed`.

title: TuffPluginTransport.abandonedPorts is an unbounded Set with no eviction
summary: Every port-confirm timeout adds a portId to `abandonedPorts`, which is only cleared in `destroy()`. The renderer transport uses a Map with age and count bounds and explains why unbounded retention is wrong.
failure_scenario: A plugin repeatedly opens a port on a channel the main process rejects. Each timeout adds a permanent string entry; since a confirm can never arrive once the main side has reaped the record, the set only ever grows across a long-running plugin session.
recommendation: Use the bounded Map-with-expiry approach already implemented in `renderer-transport.ts` (`ABANDONED_PORT_RETENTION_MS` / `ABANDONED_PORT_MAX_ENTRIES`).

title: TuffPluginTransport.destroy() leaves every on() channel registration attached
summary: `on()` creates `cleanupChannel` and returns it to the caller without storing it. `destroy()` clears only the `handlers` map, so the underlying `onMain`/`regChannel` registrations keep firing the original handlers after teardown.
failure_scenario: A plugin view registers `transport.on(PluginEvents.x, handler)` and tears down with `transport.destroy()` on unload without keeping the per-handler cleanup. The channel registration survives, so `handler` continues running against a destroyed transport on every subsequent main-process message - and re-creating the transport now double-dispatches.
recommendation: Track each `cleanupChannel` in a list and invoke them all during `destroy()`.

title: TuffPluginTransport response cache collides on non-serializable payloads
summary: `buildCacheKey` degrades to `Object.prototype.toString.call(payload)` whenever `JSON.stringify` throws, so all circular payloads for one event share a single cache entry.
failure_scenario: A plugin issues two cached sends on the same event with different circular request objects. Both hash to `"<event>:[object Object]"`, so the second call returns the first request's response without ever contacting the main process.
recommendation: Skip caching entirely when the payload cannot be serialized rather than falling back to a type-only key.

title: LoggerManager mutates the shared DEFAULT_CONFIG.modules object, so reset() never resets
summary: `{ ...DEFAULT_CONFIG }` is a shallow copy, so `config.modules` aliases the module-level `DEFAULT_CONFIG.modules`. `setModuleConfig` writes into that shared object, permanently polluting the defaults.
failure_scenario: A consumer calls `loggerManager.setModuleConfig('database', false, LogLevel.ERROR)` then `loggerManager.reset()` to restore defaults. `reset()` re-spreads `DEFAULT_CONFIG`, whose `modules` object still holds the `database` override, so the logger stays disabled and there is no way to get back to a clean state.
recommendation: Deep-clone the defaults: `{ ...DEFAULT_CONFIG, modules: {} }` in both the field initializer and `reset()`.

title: Per-module log level cannot be more verbose than the global level and is silently reverted
summary: `LogLevel` is ordered DEBUG=0 .. ERROR=3, so `Math.max(globalLevel, moduleLevel)` always selects the more restrictive level. `setModuleConfig` bypasses this and calls `logger.setLevel(level)` directly, but any later `applyConfig()` recomputes with `Math.max` and discards the override.
failure_scenario: With `globalLevel: 'warn'`, a developer calls `setModuleConfig('search-engine', true, LogLevel.DEBUG)` to debug one module. It works until the next `setConfig()` or `loadConfig()`, at which point `applyConfig` computes `Math.max(WARN, DEBUG) = WARN` and the module's debug output disappears with no warning.
recommendation: Let an explicit per-module level win outright instead of clamping it to the global level with `Math.max`.

title: TouchStorage logs an app-specific 'background.source' debug line on every hydrate and save
summary: Three unconditional `console.debug` calls in the generic, published `TouchStorage` class probe a hardcoded `(data as any)?.background?.source` field that belongs to one specific app store.
evidence: console.debug(`[TouchStorage] HYDRATE("${this.#qualifiedName}") remote version=${versionedResult.version}, background.source=`, (remoteData as any)?.background?.source)
failure_scenario: An external plugin creates a `TouchStorage('my-plugin-state', {...})` with autosave. Every keystroke-driven save prints `background.source= undefined` to the plugin's console, flooding devtools with debug output the consumer cannot disable and cannot interpret.
recommendation: Remove the debug lines or route them through the module logger at debug level.

title: Stream error delivered on the data channel never cleans up, leaking the stream registration
summary: The channel-path `data` handler reports an error and returns without calling `cleanup()`, unlike the dedicated error handler at line 215 and the MessagePort path at line 136 which both clean up.
failure_scenario: A main-process stream handler reports failure by emitting `{ error: 'quota exceeded' }` on the data channel rather than the error channel. `onError` fires, but the controller stays in `adapter.streamControllers` and all three channel registrations (`data`/`end`/`error` for that streamId) stay attached forever. Every such failed stream permanently leaks three listeners and one controller.
recommendation: Call `cleanup()` after `options.onError?.(...)` in the data-path error branch, matching the other two error paths.

title: IFeatureCommand.value allows RegExp and function values that cannot survive manifest JSON or IPC
summary: The public `IFeatureCommand.value` union includes `RegExp` and `FeatureCommandMatcher`, but features are declared in `manifest.json` and cross IPC, where both degrade to a plain string or `{}`. Only `onTrigger` is documented as non-serializable.
failure_scenario: A plugin declares `"commands": [{ "type": "regex", "value": "^calc " }]` in manifest.json, which the type permits via the string arm. The consumer casts unsoundly (`(command.value as RegExp).test(queryText)` in plugin-features-adapter.ts:60) and throws `TypeError: command.value.test is not a function`, breaking matching for that feature. The declared `'function'` command type has no matcher branch at all and silently never matches.
recommendation: Split the manifest-facing type (string patterns only) from the runtime type, and validate/compile `regex` values into a RegExp when loading the manifest.

title: useTypedChannel returns regChannel unbound, losing its `this` receiver
summary: `send` is wrapped in a closure that preserves the receiver, but `regChannel` is copied off the channel object by reference, so calling it detached loses `this`.
failure_scenario: A consumer follows the documented example, does `const c = useTypedChannel<API>()` and then `c.regChannel('config-updated', fn)`. The resolved TouchChannel is a class instance whose `regChannel` reads `this.channelMap`, so the detached call throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'channelMap')`.
recommendation: Bind it: `regChannel: channel.regChannel?.bind(channel)`.

title: levenshteinDistance allocates a full (m+1)x(n+1) matrix with no input bound
summary: The exported helper builds a complete 2D DP table rather than the standard two-row form, so memory is O(m*n) instead of O(min(m,n)), and there is no length guard on either argument.
evidence: const dp: number[][] = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, () => Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, () => 0))
failure_scenario: A plugin developer calls `levenshteinDistance(clipboardText, documentText)` on two 20,000-character strings from `@talex-touch/utils/search`. The call allocates ~400 million array slots across 20,001 nested arrays, freezing the renderer for seconds before an out-of-memory crash.
recommendation: Use the two-row rolling DP form and reject or short-circuit inputs beyond a documented maximum length.

title: ShortcutStorage.getAllShortcuts returns the internal array, letting callers corrupt unsaved state
summary: `getAllShortcuts` hands back the live `_config` array (and `getShortcutById` a live element reference), so external mutation bypasses the `_save()` that every other mutator performs.
failure_scenario: A caller does `storage.getAllShortcuts().sort(byName)` or pushes an entry to the returned array. In-memory state changes with nothing written to disk, and the mutation is then silently persisted the next time an unrelated `updateShortcutEnabled` call triggers `_save()` - so a transient UI sort becomes the saved shortcut order.
recommendation: Return a defensive copy (`[...this._config]`, deep-cloning entries) from both accessors.

title: @talex-touch/tuff-core is configured for publishing but its entry point is empty
summary: The package declares `publishConfig.access: public`, `main: dist/index.js` and `types: dist/index.d.ts`, but `src/index.ts` contains only `export {}`, there is no `dist`, no `prepublishOnly`, and no package in the monorepo depends on it.
failure_scenario: Anyone running `npm publish` in `packages/tuff-core` ships a package whose `main` and `types` point at files that were never built, so `import ... from '@talex-touch/tuff-core'` fails to resolve for every consumer. The described 'low-level build and publish primitives for Tuff' do not exist.
recommendation: Either implement the package and add a `prepublishOnly: npm run build`, or remove it from the workspace until it has content.
